question_text: A newborn is brought to the pediatric clinic by his mother because she has noticed a swelling in the belly while dressing her baby. On physical examination, the newborn is found to have a non-tender upper abdominal mass. The clinician also noticed absent irises and undescended testes in this baby. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) scan of the abdomen shows a mass of intra-renal origin. Which 1 of the following genetic disorders is most probably the cause of this neonate’s symptoms and signs?

                    ### Question
                    A newborn is brought to the pediatric clinic by his mother because she has noticed a swelling in the belly while dressing her baby. On physical examination, the newborn is found to have a non-tender upper abdominal mass. The clinician also noticed absent irises and undescended testes in this baby. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) scan of the abdomen shows a mass of intra-renal origin. Which 1 of the following genetic disorders is most probably the cause of this neonate’s symptoms and signs?

                    ### Options
                    opa. WT-1 missense mutation
opb. Deletion 11-p-13
opc. Deletion 11-p-15
opd. Duplication of 11-p-15
ope. Amplification of MYCN (N-myc) proto-oncogene

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The newborn presents with abdominal swelling and a non-tender upper abdominal mass, confirmed by MRI as intra-renal in origin. The additional findings of absent irises (aniridia) and undescended testes suggest a genetic disorder. The WT-1 gene is known to be associated with Wilms tumor, aniridia, and genitourinary anomalies, indicating that a WT-1 missense mutation is a likely cause. Deletion 11-p-13 is also associated with Wilms tumor and aniridia, making it a plausible alternative. However, deletions or duplications at 11-p-15 are not typically linked to these findings, and MYCN amplification is associated with neuroblastoma, not Wilms tumor. Therefore, the most probable cause of the neonate's symptoms is a WT-1 missense mutation, supported by the known associations of the WT-1 gene with the observed clinical features.
